newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugoslav farmers urge $357 mln debt restructuring.
newsitem.headline: Yugoslav farmers urge $357 mln debt restructuring.

text.p: Yugoslav agricultural experts on Friday issued a stark warning that the industry was on the verge of collapse and needed to restructure its crippling debts to survive.
The sector, which helped the country endure war and international sanctions, is burdened by unpaid debts and a serious shortage of cash, they said.
"Agriculture is completely exhausted by providing cheap food for the population in the past six to seven years," said Bora Djelovic, president of the Association of Agricultural Producers.

"We have appealed to the federal government to ease our difficult financial position by converting the sector's short-term outstanding liabilities into a long-term public debt," he told Reuters in an interview.

The industry's outstanding debt amounted to some two billion dinars ($357 million) at the end of last year, but Djelovic explained that only one third was principal and the rest was accumulated interest.
"We kept prices of our products at a very low levels to keep social peace and save the population from hunger but we paid the full price for the money used for financing production," he said.

Dusan Radmanovic, head of the Institute for Agriculture, said the sector simply did not have money to clear the debt. "It is a huge burden for the sector and it threatens the entire production," he added.
Agricultural producers have suggested the government take over their short-term commitments to commercial banks in exchange for an equity stake in their companies.
New debt would be issued, and paid back over ten years following a three-year grace period. Annual interest paid would be 12 percent.

"That would be a debt-for-equity swap and the state would issue dollar denominated bonds to secure creditors from eventual inflation," said Radmanovic, who headed a team commissioned to prepare the proposal soon to be discussed by the federal parliament.
The proposal already has political support, but some analysts doubted commercial banks, strapped for cash themselves, would accept the bill.

"I am sceptical the banks which face huge liquidity problems would agree as it (postponed repayments of the debt) would push them into even deeper insolvency," said a government industry source who asked not to be named.
